facts.fact_text: The first, second and third applicants live in Washington (Tyne and Wear).
The fourth applicant is an environmental group set up by the applicants.
The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to campaign against the City of Sunderland College's proposal to build on the Arena.

The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to persuade the Council not to grant the City of Sunderland College permission to build on the Arena.
On or around 14 March 1998, the first applicant, together with her husband and son, set up two stands at the entrance of the shopping mall in the Galleries.
The stands set up by the first applicant on or around 14 March 1998 displayed posters alerting the public to the likely loss of the open space known as the Arena.
The stands set up by the first applicant on or around 14 March 1998 were used to seek signatures to present to the Council on behalf of Washington First Forum.
The applicants had to remove their stands from the Galleries.
The applicants had to stop collecting signatures at the Galleries.

On 10 April 1998, the third applicant, as acting chair of Washington First Forum, wrote to the manager of the Galleries asking for permission to set up a stand and to canvass views from the public either inside the mall itself or in the adjacent car parks.
The third applicant offered to pay to be allowed to set up a stand and canvass views in the Galleries or adjacent car parks.
In his reply of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries refused the third applicant access to the Galleries and adjacent car parks.
In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that the Galleries is unique in that although it is the Town Centre, it is also privately owned.

In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that the owner's stance on all political and religious issues is one of strict neutrality and that he was charged with applying this philosophy.

At common law, any implied invitation to members of the public to enter private property may be revoked at will.
At common law, a private person's ability to eject people from his land is generally unfettered and he does not have to justify his conduct or comply with any test of reasonableness.

In Uston v. Resorts International Inc. (1982) N.J. 445A.2d 370, the Supreme Court of New Jersey laid down as a general proposition that when property owners open their premises to the general public in pursuit of their own property interests, they have no right to exclude people unreasonably but have a duty not to act in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner towards persons who come on their premises.
In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips stated that the general proposition from Uston v. Resorts International Inc. has no application in English law.

The United States Supreme Court has found that the First Amendment to the United States Federal Constitution does not require access to privately owned properties, such as shopping centres, on the basis that there has to be 'State action' (a degree of State involvement) for the amendment to apply (see, for example, Hudgens v. NLRB, 424 U.S. 507 (1976)).

In Lloyd Corp. v. Tanner (47 U.S. 551, 92 S.Ct. 2219, 33 L.Ed. 2d 131 (1972)), the United States Supreme Court held that the First Amendment to the United States Federal Constitution does not prevent a private shopping-centre owner from prohibiting distribution on its premises of leaflets unrelated to its own operations.

In Pruneyard Shopping Center v. Robbins (447 U.S. 74, 64 L.Ed. 2d 741, 100 S.Ct. 2035 (1980)), the United States Supreme Court held that permitting individuals to exercise free speech and petition rights on privately owned shopping centre property did not violate the property rights of the shopping-centre owner so long as any restriction did not amount to taking without compensation or contravene any other federal constitutional provisions.
